links.outcome: Physician accuracy with vs without LLM assistance, including poor-LLM assistance (overreliance)
links.effect: Optimal LLM raised physician accuracy (community 73.4% to 82.5%; county 84.0% to 87.9%; teaching 91.5% to 92.0%); worst LLM lowered accuracy below baseline, inappropriate regimens 26.6% to 35.2%.
links.quote: The worst LLM configurations decreased physician performance below baseline, increasing inappropriate regimen rates from 26.6% to 35.2% across all levels.

links.outcome: Whether physicians detected incorrect AI outputs / automation bias
links.effect: With the worst model, accuracy declined for all six physicians (e.g., Physician 2 to 62.3%); case review showed automation bias with unnecessary escalation to drug therapy or downgrading of combination therapy.
links.quote: Furthermore, a case-level review revealed classic automation bias: lifestyle-only strategies were unnecessarily escalated to drug therapy based on erroneous LLM suggestions, while guideline-concordant initial dual therapy was sometimes downgraded to monotherapy for patients who clearly qualified for combination treatment.

links.outcome: Human-AI team performance versus unassisted physicians in intended workflow
links.effect: Optimal LLM assistance improved accuracy for five of six physicians (e.g., Physician 1 to 84.3%, Physician 2 to 80.7%); worst-model assistance reduced accuracy for all participants.
links.quote: When the optimal model was integrated into physicians’ decision-making workflows, five physicians demonstrated improved accuracy compared with their standalone performance.

links.outcome: Regimen selection appropriateness including dosing and implausible drugs
links.effect: Worst model generated implausible drug names/combinations; regimen-level performance weaker than upstream decisions; unsafe outputs included contraindicated combinations and inadequate dosing.
links.quote: These unsafe outputs manifested distinct clinical patterns, including contraindicated drug combinations, inadequate dosing for high-risk patients, and failure to integrate critical comorbidities such as chronic kidney disease or heart failure.

links.outcome: Guideline-concordance of LLM treatment recommendations
links.effect: Zero-shot accuracy ~62.7-65.0% vs up to 91.3% with guidance prompts; regimen selection remained a persistent challenge with neutral or incomplete regimens.
links.quote: Even with optimal guidance prompt, models frequently produced neutral or incomplete regimens, particularly for patients with multiple comorbidities or advanced cardiovascular risk 8 .

links.outcome: LLM accuracy compared against physicians and across models/prompts on same cases
links.effect: Best configuration (GPT-4.1 Guidance-Self-Consistency, 91.3%) matched top physicians (92.7%) and exceeded community physicians; zero-shot DeepSeek 62.6%.
links.quote: Overall, GPT-4.1 with the Guidance-Self-Consistency prompt proved to be the most effective model-prompt configuration, achieving the optimal accuracy of 91.3% across the main decision-making dimensions; thus, it was selected as the optimal model.

links.outcome: LLM performance variation across prompt phrasing strategies
links.effect: Accuracy varied widely across 18 prompt strategies, e.g., ChatGPT-4.1 64.0% zero-shot vs 91.3% Guidance-Self-Consistency.
links.quote: Across the 4 LLMs and 18 prompt engineering strategies, we observed a broad spectrum of performance, highlighting that both the choice of model and the design of prompts significantly influence clinical decision outcomes.

unlisted_practices: Structured guideline-based prompt engineering (guidance prompts, self-consistency, chain-of-thought) to improve LLM clinical decision accuracy

openai.sample_unit: simulated hypertension cases reviewed by 6 physicians

links.outcome: Task 1 accuracy by prompt strategy
links.effect: ChatGPT-4.1 accuracy was 91.3% with Guidance-Self-Consistency versus 64.0% zero-shot.
links.quote: Specifically, with the Guidance-Self-Consistency strategy, ChatGPT-4.1 achieved an accuracy of 91.3% for Task 1, while it only reached 64.0% under zero-shot prompting.

links.outcome: LLM treatment decision accuracy and hallucinations
links.effect: DeepSeek zero-shot had lowest accuracy, 62.6%, and highest risk of hallucinations and inconsistencies.
links.quote: In contrast, DeepSeek with a plain zero-shot prompt demonstrated the lowest accuracy at 62.6% and exhibited the highest risk of hallucinations and inconsistencies, and was therefore selected as the worst model.

links.outcome: physician accuracy with AI assistance
links.effect: Optimal LLM improved average accuracy: community 73.4% to 82.5%, county 84.0% to 87.9%, teaching 91.5% to 92.0%.
links.quote: Optimal LLM assistance consistently enhanced physicians' average accuracy across all levels (community hospital: 73.4% to 82.5%; county hospital: 84.0% to 87.9%; teaching hospital: 91.5% to 92.0%) and reduced inappropriate regimen rates.

links.outcome: automation bias in regimen selection
links.effect: Worst-model assistance increased inappropriate regimens: P1 43.4%, P2 47.4%, P3 36.2%, P4 35.5%, P5 23.7%, P6 25.0%.
links.quote: Furthermore, a case-level review revealed classic automation bias: lifestyle-only strategies were unnecessarily escalated to drug therapy based on erroneous LLM suggestions, while guideline-concordant initial dual therapy was sometimes downgraded to monotherapy for patients who clearly qualified for combination treatment.

links.outcome: decision accuracy with worst LLM advice
links.effect: Accuracy fell to 67.3%, 62.3%, 71.7%, 73.7%, 87.3%, and 83.3% for Physicians 1-6.
links.quote: Accuracy decreased to 67.3% for Physician 1, 62.3% for Physician 2, 71.7% for Physician 3, 73.7% for Physician 4, 87.3% for Physician 5, and 83.3% for Physician 6.

unlisted_practices: Guidance-based prompt engineering with self-consistency and structured reasoning frameworks for hypertension treatment recommendations
